header: Attendees: Maya, Ethan, Luis (Redwood); Priya, Tom, Sara, Eric (AstraHealth)
summary: Weekly pilot sync focused on SDK invoke patterns, function/tool calling, and structured JSON output parsing in AstraHealth staging environment.
Discussed current test results: stable responses but occasional malformed JSON from streaming mode; p95 latency around 300-420ms depending on batching and model variant.
Agreed on next steps: run more targeted E2E benchmarks with streaming+function-calls, share webhook parse examples, and circulate pricing/security docs to unblock pilot expansion.
topics: Function / tool calling reliability and idempotency
Structured output (schema enforcement + recovery from malformed JSON)
Security: KMS, audit logs, and RBAC for webhook tooling
transcript: [00:00] Maya Chen: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick run through agenda, SDK invoke patterns, function calls, structured output issues you saw last week.

[00:15] Priya Sethi: Yep thanks. We had three things in staging: streaming enabled, function-calling to invoke our billing tool, and JSON schema validation on the response. Some runs passed, some failed with truncated json.
[00:32] Ethan Park: When you say truncated JSON, is that in streaming mode only or also in non-streaming?
[00:38] Tom Alvarez: Mostly streaming, yeah. Non-streaming looks okay but we did see one case where the assistant returned double-encoded JSON like a stringified payload.
[00:52] Sara Ng: I think for the double-encode the client SDK we used was the rust-sdk wrapper, might be doing an extra JSON.escape somewhere — we need to check.

[01:05] Ethan Park: Got it. A couple of notes: streaming can interleave tokens and if your parser expects the full top-level JSON immediately it can throw. We typically recommend using the SDK's streaming-json helper that buffers until a valid parse is found, or using function-calls which return a separate structured payload.

[01:28] Priya Sethi: We tried function-calls but the billing tool invocation failed a few times — the tool endpoint returned 5xx intermittently and Redwood retried which made duplicate side-effects. Need idempotency keys.

[01:44] Maya Chen: Important callout. Redwood's function-calling layer supports idempotency tokens if you pass a request_id in the call metadata; SE note you can wire that from your webhook. Ethan, remind them the current retry policy?

[01:58] Ethan Park: By default the runtime does a single automated retry on 5xx for short-lived requests, but for function-calls we can turn off auto-retry so the app can handle idempotency. On Dedicated you have finer control; in Hosted you can set per-route policies.
[02:15] Eric Lowe: Can we log the idempotency token in audit logs? We need traceability for compliance.
[02:20] Luis Ortega: Yes, audit logs include token, route, model version. We'll send a sample log schema.
[02:35] Tom Alvarez: Back to malformed JSON, what's the mitigation if streaming returns partial payloads?

[02:41] Ethan Park: Two practical routes: (1) Use function-calls so the model returns a structured JSON object field that the runtime guarantees as complete, or (2) use the SDK streaming-json helper that accumulates token chunks until parsable. Also, add a fallback parser that attempts to close braces and re-parse — it's not pretty but works for predictable schemas.
[03:02] Priya Sethi: We prefer function-calls for critical operations like billing, but for free-text summarization we want streaming for latency. So mixed approach per-route.

[03:14] Maya Chen: Sounds reasonable. Also, consider schema validation on the backend — if function-calls come back with unknown fields, fail fast and surface to user. We can share example JSON schema and validators.
[03:30] Sara Ng: Question on SDKs — we tried the Python SDK and saw different timeout defaults than Node. Which defaults should we rely on?

[03:40] Ethan Park: Defaults differ historically; best practice is to set explicit timeouts in your client. For streaming, set read timeout to 90s, for sync short calls 10s. We'll add these recommended settings to the integration doc.
[03:55] Tom Alvarez: Also saw memory blowups when KV cache got large on the client side with long-context tests — any recommended cache size?

[04:03] Ethan Park: The runtime manages KV cache server-side; client-side you may be keeping a separate transcript. Keep local caches shallow (<4k tokens) unless you have explicit eviction. The 'K-V cash' in the transcript — sorry, K-V cache — is tuned per-model. We'll share tuning knobs.

[04:24] Priya Sethi: Could you summarize the performance numbers from last week's run? Our sheet shows p50 ~120ms, p95 ~360ms for the 1.3B model with batching=auto, streaming=true. but p95 jumped to 420ms in spikes.

[04:38] Ethan Park: Right. Spikes corresponded to background quantization compaction job on the Dedicated pool we used briefly; also larger sequence lengths cause kernel selection to change. For short responses, p95 of 300-350ms is achievable with batching=auto and quant 8-bit. We'll annotate the sheet with the job timestamps.
[04:58] Priya Sethi: Is dedicated pool required for stable latency? We're considering Dedicated pilot but cost is a concern.

[05:06] Maya Chen: For strict SLOs, Dedicated gives predictability and isolation. Hosted can meet many use cases but has more variance. We can propose a hybrid routing policy — critical calls to Dedicated, non-critical to Hosted to balance cost.
[05:22] Tom Alvarez: About tool calling security: how do we ensure the model doesn't leak PII to tool endpoints or vice versa?

[05:28] Luis Ortega: We recommend request-level redaction filters on the Redwood side and TLS mutual auth for internal tool endpoints. Also pass minimal context to tools and store full logs only in encrypted buckets with KMS. We'll include the SSO/KMS notes.

[05:45] Sara Ng: For our structured output, we attempted to use a top-level schema like {action: string, payload: {..}} — sometimes payload keys come back in different order and strict parsers fail. Any suggestions?

[05:57] Ethan Park: Ordering shouldn't matter for JSON, but if your parser is brittle, switch to tolerant parsing or validate fields rather than exact string match. Also consider using function-calls with explicit parameter types (Redwood runtime maps those to JSON automatically).
[06:10] Priya Sethi: Can function-calls return nested arrays securely? We need to return a list of billing items.
[06:16] Ethan Park: Yes, nested arrays and objects are supported. The runtime will surface the function return in a dedicated field rather than as raw text, which avoids streaming truncation issues.
[06:28] Tom Alvarez: We hit an edge where model returned a 'null' where we expected an array and our ingest crashed. How to guard?
[06:34] Maya Chen: Defensive coding: treat fields optional, use schema with defaults, and implement circuit-breakers. We'll share a small 'resilient parser' example.
[06:46] Eric Lowe: One more infra ask: Can Redwood emit per-request timing headers so we can correlate in our APM?
[06:52] Luis Ortega: Yes, we can include x-rw-latency-ms and x-rw-cache-hit headers. We'll provide header spec and example curl.
[07:05] Priya Sethi: About telemetry — we need token-level cost breakout to justify pilot costs. Does your console show per-route cost for function-calls?
[07:14] Maya Chen: Redwood Console shows token-level breakdown and per-route dashboards. Function-calls are billed by compute + tool-exec time; we'll share a screenshot and a billing example.
[07:29] Sara Ng: On the SDK side, is there a recommended backoff strategy for function-calls?
[07:35] Ethan Park: Exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 attempts client-side. Turn off server-side automatic retry for side-effecting calls. Use idempotency keys.
[07:48] Tom Alvarez: Tom: We'll need a sample idempotency header format.
[07:53] Luis Ortega: Format: X-Request-Id: <uuid>, plus X-Idempotency-Key if you want a separate key. We'll drop examples in the doc.
[08:04] Priya Sethi: A quick dev question: we use open-source parsers that choke on trailing commas — streaming sometimes ends with extra comma due to partial output. Any automatic cleaner?
[08:13] Ethan Park: The SDK streaming helper trims trailing commas and attempts to balance braces; it's a pragmatic patch. For mission-critical flows use function-calls.
[08:26] Maya Chen: Let's talk rollback/validation — you mentioned a canary that failed last week. What happened?

[08:33] Tom Alvarez: Canary to 5% traffic hit a model variant that had a new tokenizer setting; led to tokenization mismatch and off-by-one in the payload. We rolled back. Need model pinning per-route.
[08:45] Ethan Park: Model pinning is supported; you can pin by model id and model-version. We'll show example config in the routing policy doc.
[08:58] Priya Sethi: Anything else about batching? We saw throughput improvements with batching=auto but also higher tail latency for single-user flows.

[09:07] Ethan Park: Batching increases throughput but can add queueing delay. For low-latency customer-facing endpoints, set max_batch_size small or use latency-first policy. For background jobs, batch larger. We'll propose per-route policies in the next doc iteration.

[09:26] Maya Chen: Alright let's recap actions. Ethan will run the E2E benchmark with streaming + function-calls enabled; Maya will send pricing and security docs; Tom will post webhook parser. Anything to add?
[09:38] Priya Sethi: Please include examples for turning off server retries for side-effecting calls.
[09:43] Ethan Park: Noted — I'll include config snippets for Hosted and Dedicated.
[09:50] Luis Ortega: Sharing audit log schema and header spec after the call.
[09:55] Sara Ng: Quick follow: can we get a short sample of the resilient parser? Even pseudo code is fine.
[10:02] Maya Chen: We'll add a small Python/Node resilient parser snippets in the shared gist. Luis will own.
[10:10] Tom Alvarez: Okay thanks all. We'll reconvene next Thursday same time unless we have blockers.
[10:15] Maya Chen: Thanks, ending recording — will send meeting notes and links.
